html:
Today is Lichun, the Beginning of Spring in the traditional Chinese calendar, and the weather played along: much warmer than the past few days. Out with Dad in the morning, I barely needed a hat.

Dad and I got to the “You’re So Pretty” hair salon at 8:10, and six or seven people were already waiting. After five minutes we gave up on the line and decided to come back tomorrow. Then we went to the supermarket. Going down the steps, I reached into my pocket for my phone, lost my concentration and nearly fell. Me falling would be no big deal, but there was an old man just in front of me, and that would have been no joke.

While we were picking out vegetables, there was a sudden roar. Listening more closely, I worked out that an auntie had got into a fight with the clerk who weighs and prices the produce (in Chinese supermarkets, staff do that at a counter). As far as I could make out, there was only one person ahead of her in line, and the clerk had been rude to her. Her grandson hauled her away, but in less than a minute she was back for round two, marched right up to the clerk, launched into the national curse, and looked ready to start swinging. Bystanders hurried to pull her away, above all her grandson (son’s son or daughter’s son, I couldn’t tell), who did his very best to block her, pleading, exasperated and close to tears, “Stop it! Just stop!” When they finally got her away, her mouth was as busy as ever, and an old man nearby raised the stakes: “That woman’s not right in the head.” Later, when I went over to have my things weighed, the clerk and her coworker were grumbling helplessly: “Good grief, she was acting like a f***ing lunatic.”

We bought a few things. At the checkout, Dad glanced over at the nuts and dried fruit section and whispered to me, “Look at that old guy, stuffing nuts into his pockets by the handful.” I said, “With that many handfuls, he’s set for New Year.”

Back home, I did Baduanjin with Mom (the “Eight Brocades,” a gentle qigong routine), plus tai chi and another of those exercise routines popular with older people. Then twenty push-ups and three sets of planks. At last I had worked up a sweat. Satisfied.

In the afternoon I took my nephew, my cousin’s son, to play pool. The last time I saw him was in September 2017, when he was a little squirt in fifth grade. Now he is a strapping eighteen-year-old and taller than me. His parents divorced when he was small, and he grew up shuttling between four places: Nanjing, Tianjin, Tieling and K County. During the pandemic, when school kept moving online, his grades slipped like so many other kids’. Unlike so many other kids, he chose to drop out. For a number of reasons he developed psychological problems and had suicidal thoughts. After dropping out, billiards became his way forward, something he could focus on. My cousin says something I once said saved her. I barely remember it myself; it was roughly that university isn’t the only path. Now he is training in Tianjin and wants to make a name for himself in billiards.

In the evening we brought him home for dinner. He doesn’t talk much with my parents, but he has plenty to say to me. Mom said that sometimes when she visits his home (he lives with his grandparents), he won’t even come out of his room. His mother remarried, to a K County local eleven years younger than her and three years younger than me, so my nephew doesn’t live with them; he lives at his grandparents’. After dinner we chatted for a while, and then he went out with his girlfriend. She had dropped by while we were playing pool, very politely called me “Uncle” when she saw me, and said goodbye to me when she left.

Four years without coming back to China because of the pandemic, and suddenly I feel old. In those four years my nephews and nieces have become strapping young men and young women, with boyfriends and girlfriends of their own. No wonder my parents now call themselves old folks: in the kids’ eyes they are old, no question, and I have become a bona fide member of the older generation.

These four years have changed a lot. As for how deep those changes go, what I see may not be the whole picture. Time will tell.
